lead: American painter and printmaker (1844-1926) who lived in Paris and showed with the Impressionists; known for soft pastels and flat color.
paras: Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh, studied in Philadelphia, and settled in Paris in the 1870s. At Edgar Degas's invitation she joined the Impressionist group and showed with them in several of their exhibitions.
The chapters below follow her training, her Impressionist years and her later color prints and pastels, and end with the archive's numbers.

chapters.title: Pittsburgh and Paris
chapters.text:
Cassatt grew up near Pittsburgh and studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia before going to Europe. She worked in Paris and elsewhere, copying old masters, and had works accepted at the Salon.

By the middle 1870s she had settled in Paris, and her early color is still that of the Salon: warm browns and reds with {{Bistre}} shadows.

chapters.title: The Impressionist years
chapters.text:
Degas invited her to join the group, and she showed with the Impressionists in several of their exhibitions. Her scenes of women and children, in the theater box and at tea, use pale skin and cloth set against soft green and blue grounds.

Her pastels keep their color well, since pastel is nearly pure pigment, so the surfaces are closer to what she made than many oils of her time. Soft {{Powder Blue}} and {{Dusty Rose}} come up often.

chapters.title: Color prints and flat color
chapters.text:
A large Japanese woodblock print exhibition in Paris in 1890 is widely credited with changing her approach, and her color prints that followed use flat areas and clear outlines.

Compare a pastel with one of these prints. The first blends colors by hand into a hazy field; the second sets a few colors down in separate flat shapes.
chapters.pull: The pastel blends by hand; the print sets a few flat colors side by side.

chapters.title: What our archive shows
chapters.text:
Our archive holds only 123 Cassatt paintings, so these findings are tentative. They are photographs of varnished or framed works, not measurements of pigment.

She used very dark olive browns, {{Bistre}} and {{Café Noir}} about a third as often as her peers, and her darkest areas are {{Smoky Black}} and {{Black Blue}}. Her lightest are Tan, greyish white and {{Dawn Grey}}.
